findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "available", "prototype").
findings.evidence: lib sets the available built-in typings (e.g. ["ES2023", "DOM"]); it defaults from target, so using Array.prototype.at or fetch types without matching lib gives 'property does not exist' errors even though the runtime has them
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: Several bullets mix more than one idea, and the node16/nodenext row says nothing about extensions in CJS files.
findings.evidence: "Syntax the target supports is kept as-is; newer syntax is downleveled"; "No polyfills added; lib controls the typings"; "lib defaults from target: .at() types missing → property does not exist"
findings.fix: Split each into one-idea bullets. Rewrite the lib line as "lib defaults come from target; a target that is too old makes .at() fail with 'property does not exist'".

findings.summary: The paths bullets pack more than one idea, and the JSON snippet comes before the idea behind it.
findings.evidence: "Works without baseUrl since TS 4.1" / "Relative targets resolve from the tsconfig file" followed immediately by the json block; "Editor happy, build says Cannot find module: bundler alias never set"
findings.fix: State the idea first ("paths maps @/* to ./src/* for the type-checker only"), then show the code. Split the 'Editor happy' bullet into the symptom and the cause.

findings.summary: The augmentation example targets 'express-serve-static-core', while the outline and the surrounding text talk about augmenting 'express'. The page does not explain the change, so a learner who writes declare module 'express' may find it doesn't work.
findings.fix: Add a note that Express's Request interface is defined in express-serve-static-core, so that is the module name to augment. Or use declare module 'express' as the outline does, if that is the intended teaching.

findings.summary: Packed bullets, and the augmentation code is shown before the idea behind it.
findings.evidence: "3. Augmentation" starts with the typescript block; the explanation "top-level import makes this file a module, so it merges" comes after it; "No top-level import/export: global ambient, replaces not augments"
findings.fix: Open section 3 with the one-line idea ("a module file with declare module merges into the existing types"). Put that line before the code, then split the import/ambient bullets.

findings.summary: verbatimModuleSyntax is taught first and says it "Implies isolatedModules safety", but isolatedModules is not defined until the next section.
findings.evidence: Section 1: "Implies isolatedModules safety"; isolatedModules is only introduced in section 2: "Errors on code a single-file transpiler (esbuild, SWC, Babel) can't compile"
findings.fix: Put the isolatedModules section first, as the page title does, and then present verbatimModuleSyntax as the simpler rule that builds on it.

findings.summary: The isolatedModules section never says why a single-file transpiler needs the type-only rules, so the two rules (export type, const enum) read as arbitrary.
findings.evidence: "Re-export a type with export type { T }" and "const enum use is restricted", with no mention that each file must be understood alone
findings.fix: Add one line: a single-file transpiler cannot see other files, so it cannot tell whether `export { T }` re-exports a type (to erase) or a value (to keep). The same limit applies to const enum inlining.

findings.summary: The code is shown before its idea, and the CommonJS error bullets read as a stray sequence.
findings.evidence: "ESM syntax with module: CommonJS is an error" / "Fix: module: NodeNext plus \"type\": \"module\" in package.json" / "Or write import x = require('x')"; "Implies isolatedModules safety"
findings.fix: Group the CommonJS error and its two fixes under one labelled line, e.g. 'Error: ESM syntax with module: CommonJS' with 'Fix 1' and 'Fix 2'. Reword 'Implies isolatedModules safety' as 'It enforces isolatedModules rules, so one flag covers both'.

findings.summary: The first answer is muddled: it states the emit result in a confusing way and gives no reason.
findings.evidence: "import { type User } is emitted as the side-effect import import {} from './user'." / "Use import type when the whole import should vanish."
findings.fix: Lead with the contrast: 'import type is erased completely; import { type User } leaves a bare import {} from "./user" that still loads the module for its side effects.'
